learn.title: Numbers have limits
learn.body: A variable has a fixed size, so it can only hold a limited range of numbers. A 4-byte `int` holds about minus 2.1 billion up to 2.1 billion. Go past the edge and the result is not what maths says.

learn.title: Wrapping around
learn.body: An unsigned char holds 0 to 255. Adding 1 to 255 wraps to 0.

learn.title: Signed overflow
learn.body: For unsigned types, wrapping is defined: the value restarts at 0. For a signed `int`, going past the maximum is undefined behaviour. It often wraps to a large negative number, but the language promises nothing. Avoid it.

learn.title: Using a bigger type
learn.body: If a result may be large, use a bigger type. The second part of the program above casts to `long long`, which holds 8 bytes. `2000000000 * 2` is then a correct 4000000000. Print it with `%lld`.

learn.title: Decimals are approximate
learn.body: Computers store decimals in binary, so 0.1 is not exact.

learn.title: Never compare floats with ==
learn.body: 0.1 + 0.2 is stored as 0.30000000000000004, so `== 0.3` is false (0). Instead check that the two numbers are very close: `fabs(a - b) < 1e-9`. Also, converting a decimal to int drops the decimals, so 3.9 becomes 3.

learn.title: Why the sum is not exact
steps: 0.1 is stored as a nearby binary fraction, a hair above 0.1
0.2 is stored the same way, a hair above 0.2
Their sum lands a hair above 0.3, so `== 0.3` is false

learn.body: Use whole numbers for counting and money in cents. Use decimals for measurements, and expect tiny errors.

questions.prompt: `unsigned char c = 255; c = c + 1;` What does `c` hold?
questions.explanation: An unsigned char wraps around from 255 back to 0.

questions.prompt: Is signed `int` overflow well defined in C?
choices: Yes, it always gives an error message
Yes, it stops the program safely
questions.explanation: Only unsigned wrapping is guaranteed. Signed overflow is undefined.

questions.prompt: What is the safest way to hold `2000000000 * 2`?
questions.explanation: `long long` is large enough to hold 4000000000.

questions.prompt: What does `printf("%d", 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3);` print on a typical computer? Type the digit.
questions.explanation: A false comparison gives 0 in C. The sum is 0.30000000000000004, not 0.3.

questions.prompt: To compare two doubles, test that the \_\_ of their difference is tiny.
questions.explanation: `fabs(a - b) < 1e-9` asks whether they are nearly equal.

questions.prompt: `double h = 3.9; int x = h;` What does `x` hold?
questions.explanation: Converting a decimal to int drops the fractional part. It does not round.

questions.prompt: `0.1` cannot be stored exactly because computers store decimals in \_\_.
questions.explanation: Many decimals have no exact finite binary form, so they are slightly off.

questions.prompt: Match each type to its safe use.
questions.explanation: Pick a type big enough for the numbers you expect.
